blocks.text:
Design a Library Management System that lets members check out physical copies of books. A book title may have several physical copies. Checkout must be blocked when a member has too many active loans or too much unpaid fine balance. When every copy of a title is checked out, a member joins a hold queue instead of being turned away, and is automatically granted the next available copy when one is returned. Returning a copy computes an overdue fine, capped at a maximum per loan so a badly overdue book cannot generate an unbounded charge.

  • Actors: Member (checks out, returns books), LibraryService (the core orchestrator).
  • Scope: a single branch catalog with multiple copies per title, loan-limit and fine-limit eligibility, hold queues, and capped overdue fines.

The distinguishing mechanic is a fine-balance eligibility gate (a member with too much unpaid fine cannot borrow more, regardless of loan count) combined with a per-loan fine cap, layered ahead of the familiar per-copy checkout and FIFO hold-queue mechanic.
The system must support the following core capabilities:

items: Catalog: define books, each with a category (REGULAR, PREMIUM) and one or more physical copies.
Checkout: a member requests a book; the system assigns an available copy if the member is eligible.
Eligibility: a checkout is blocked if the member already has too many active loans, or too much unpaid fine balance.
Hold queue: if the member is eligible but no copy is free, the member joins a FIFO hold queue for that title.
Return: returning a copy computes an overdue fine (capped) and, if the hold queue is non-empty, automatically grants the copy to the longest-waiting member.

blocks.text: Beyond correctness, the design should hold up along five quality pillars:

metadata.alt: Five non-functional pillars: scalability, extensibility, maintainability, performance, thread safety

items: Scalability: supporting many books, copies, and members must not require touching existing checkout logic.
Extensibility: new eligibility rules or fine schemes should plug in without rewriting the service.
Maintainability: eligibility checking, notification, and copy creation are isolated in their own classes.
Performance: finding a free copy is O(copies of that title), which stays small in practice.
Thread safety: two members checking out the last copy of a title concurrently must not both succeed.

blocks.text: Questions worth asking the interviewer before designing:

items: Should the loan-limit and fine-limit thresholds be configurable per member tier, or fixed system-wide?
Should a promoted hold recheck the member's eligibility (loans, fines) at promotion time, in case it changed while waiting?
Is there a maximum hold-queue length per title, or is it unbounded?
Should fines be paid explicitly (reducing outstandingFines), or does that happen outside this system's scope?
Should reference-only (non-circulating) books be modeled as a category that can never be checked out?

blocks.text: To keep the design focused, we make these explicit assumptions:

items: Loan duration and fine rate depend only on the book's category (REGULAR: 14-day loan, 0.5 per day fine, capped at 5; PREMIUM: 7-day loan, 1.0 per day fine, capped at 10).

Eligibility (loan limit, fine limit) is checked at both checkout time and hold-placement time, but not re-checked when a held member is later promoted, matching the same simplification used in Course Registration System.
Paying down outstandingFines is out of scope; this design only accrues fines on return.
The hold queue is unbounded, like Course Registration System's waitlist, not capacity-bounded like Airline Management System's overbooking limit.

blocks.text: The design centers on five core entities:

metadata.alt: Core entities: Book, BookCopy, BookCategory, Member, Loan, Hold Queue

items: Book: a catalog title with a category driving loan duration and fine rate.
BookCopy: one physical copy with a status (AVAILABLE, CHECKED_OUT).
BookCategory: an enum (REGULAR, PREMIUM).
Member: tracks outstanding fine balance.
Loan: ties a member to a copy, with checkout day, due day, and fine.

blocks.text: These entities connect through a small set of well-defined relationships:

metadata.alt: A book has many copies and one hold queue; a member makes many loans; a loan references exactly one copy

items: Book to BookCopy is one-to-many.
Book to Hold Queue is one-to-one, one queue per title.
Member to Loan is one-to-many.
Loan to BookCopy is many-to-one.

blocks.text: Three patterns keep eligibility, notification, and copy creation decoupled from the core service.
Why needed: loan limits, fine limits, loan durations, and fine rates are all policy decisions that change independently of the checkout workflow.

Why it is the best fit: a new policy (e.g., a stricter fine cap during a fine amnesty period) is a new strategy implementation, with zero changes to LibraryService. What it solves: it isolates frequently-revised library policy from stable orchestration logic.
Why needed: loan creation, rejection, holds, and returns are all events a real library system would want to react to (email reminders, fine statements).

metadata.alt: LibraryObserver interface notified by LibraryService on every lifecycle event

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: LibraryService does not need to know who is listening. What it solves: it decouples the core checkout workflow from side effects.
Why needed: copy id generation should not be scattered across catalog setup code.
Why it is the best fit: acquiring more copies of a popular title becomes a single factory call. What it solves: centralizes id-generation rules so they cannot drift or collide.
Each class has a single, clear responsibility:

items: Book: attributes bookId, title, category; responsibility: describe a catalog title.
BookCopy: attributes copyId, bookId, status; responsibility: track whether one physical copy is free.
BookCopyFactory: method createCopies(book, count); responsibility: generate title-prefixed copy ids.
Member: attributes memberId, name, outstandingFines; responsibility: track fine balance relevant to eligibility.
Loan: attributes loanId, memberId, copyId, checkoutDay, dueDay, fine, status; responsibility: capture one loan end-to-end.
LibraryService: the orchestrator; responsibility: check eligibility, assign or hold copies, compute fines on return, process hold promotions, and notify observers.

blocks.text: Two interfaces keep the design open for extension:

metadata.alt: BorrowingEligibilityStrategy and LibraryObserver interfaces with their key methods

items: BorrowingEligibilityStrategy: checkEligibility(member, activeLoanCount): returns null if eligible, or a rejection reason string; also supplies loanDurationDays and fineForDaysLate by category.
LibraryObserver: onLoanCreated / onLoanRejected / onHoldPlaced / onLoanReturned: abstracts away who reacts to lifecycle events.

blocks.text: The end-to-end happy path, alongside its rejection and hold branches, looks like this:

metadata.alt: Check eligibility, check copy availability, confirm or hold; return computes fine and may promote

items: Happy path: checkout → eligible → copy free → ACTIVE loan with due date set.
Rejection path: checkout → loan limit reached or fine limit exceeded → rejected.
Hold path: checkout → eligible → no copy free → join FIFO hold queue.
Return path: return → compute fine from days late (capped) → free the copy → if hold queue non-empty, promote the longest-waiting member into a new loan.

blocks.text: The service exposes a small, intention-revealing API:

items: checkout(memberId, bookId): validates eligibility, then assigns a copy or joins the hold queue, or throws if ineligible.
returnBook(loanId, returnDay): computes and applies the overdue fine, frees the copy, and promotes a held member if applicable.

blocks.text: Three custom exceptions cover the realistic failure modes:

items: BorrowingNotEligibleException: the member has too many active loans or too much unpaid fine balance.
InvalidLoanException: an unknown member, book, or loan id.
LoanNotActiveException: returnBook is called on a loan that is not currently ACTIVE (already returned).

blocks.text: The critical race is two members checking out the last available copy of a title at the same moment.

metadata.alt: Two threads racing for the last copy; synchronization ensures only one is confirmed and the other joins the hold queue

blocks.text: Synchronizing the copy-search-and-assign step per book ensures the check and the status update happen atomically, so only one checkout can ever claim the last copy.
The pattern choices make several future features low-friction to add:

items: A new eligibility rule (membership tier, age restriction) is a new BorrowingEligibilityStrategy implementation.
A new notification channel (SMS, due-date reminder emails) is a new LibraryObserver implementation.
A new book category (REFERENCE, never circulating) is a new enum value plus a rule in the eligibility strategy.
A payment feature to reduce outstandingFines can be added as a new service method without touching checkout or return logic.
Single Responsibility: BookCopy tracks state, BorrowingEligibilityStrategy decides eligibility and fines, LibraryObserver reacts to events, each for one reason to change.
Open/Closed: new eligibility or notification behavior extends via new classes, not edits to LibraryService.
Liskov Substitution: any BorrowingEligibilityStrategy or LibraryObserver implementation can replace another without breaking the service.
Interface Segregation: LibraryObserver exposes only the four lifecycle callbacks a listener actually needs.
Dependency Inversion: LibraryService depends on the BorrowingEligibilityStrategy and LibraryObserver interfaces, not concrete classes.
A book returned exactly on its due day accrues no fine.
A fine that would exceed the category's cap is clamped to the cap rather than growing unbounded.
A member exactly at the loan limit (not over it) is still rejected, since the check is "at or above" the max.
Returning the same loan twice throws LoanNotActiveException on the second call.
checkout: O(copies of the title) to find a free copy, plus O(active loans of the member) for the eligibility count.
returnBook: O(1) to free the copy and compute the fine, plus O(1) to pop the head of the hold queue.
Space: O(copies + loans + held) held in memory.

blocks.text: A relational schema mirrors the in-memory model directly, with foreign keys enforcing referential integrity:

metadata.alt: ER diagram: Book, BookCopy, Member, Loan

items: An index on BookCopy(bookId, status) speeds up the "find a free copy of this title" query.
An index on Loan(memberId, status) speeds up counting a member's active loans for eligibility checks.
Re-check eligibility at hold-promotion time in case the member's loan count or fine balance changed while waiting.
Add an explicit payFine(memberId, amount) method to reduce outstandingFines.
Support renewals (extending the due date) when no hold exists for the title.
In a distributed deployment, move copy-status locking to a database-level row lock or a distributed lock rather than in-process synchronization.

# Observer interface: reacts to library lifecycle events.
class LibraryObserver:
    def on_loan_created(self, loan): raise NotImplementedError
    def on_loan_rejected(self, member_id, reason): raise NotImplementedError
    def on_hold_placed(self, member_id, book_id): raise NotImplementedError
    def on_loan_returned(self, loan, fine): raise NotImplementedError

# Simple observer that prints events to the console.
class ConsoleLibraryObserver(LibraryObserver):
    def on_loan_created(self, loan):
        print(f"Loan {loan.loan_id} created for {loan.member_id}, copy {loan.copy_id}, due day {loan.due_day}")

    def on_loan_rejected(self, member_id, reason):
        print(f"Checkout rejected for {member_id}: {reason}")

    def on_hold_placed(self, member_id, book_id):
        print(f"Hold placed for {member_id} on book {book_id}")

    def on_loan_returned(self, loan, fine):
        print(f"Loan {loan.loan_id} returned by {loan.member_id}, fine {fine}")

# Custom exceptions for the realistic failure modes.
class BorrowingNotEligibleException(Exception): pass
class InvalidLoanException(Exception): pass
class LoanNotActiveException(Exception): pass

# The core orchestrator tying every piece together.
class LibraryService:
    def __init__(self, eligibility_strategy):
        self.books = {}          # bookId -> Book
        self.copies = {}         # copyId -> BookCopy
        self.members = {}        # memberId -> Member
        self.loans = {}          # loanId -> Loan
        self.holds = {}          # bookId -> FIFO queue of memberIds
        self.eligibility_strategy = eligibility_strategy  # pluggable policy
        self.observers = []       # listeners
        self.loan_counter = 0     # simple id generator

    def add_book(self, book):
        self.books[book.book_id] = book  # register a book
        self.holds[book.book_id] = []      # init its hold queue

    def add_copies(self, new_copies):
        for c in new_copies:
            self.copies[c.copy_id] = c  # register a copy

    def add_member(self, member):
        self.members[member.member_id] = member  # register a member

    def add_observer(self, observer):
        self.observers.append(observer)  # register a listener

    def _active_loan_count(self, member_id):
        count = 0                                                # running total
        for l in self.loans.values():                             # scan all loans
            if l.member_id == member_id and l.status == "ACTIVE":
                count += 1                                            # count active ones
        return count  # total active loans for this member

    def _find_free_copy(self, book_id):
        for c in self.copies.values():                             # scan all copies
            if c.book_id == book_id and c.is_available():
                return c  # first free copy of this title
        return None  # no free copy

    def checkout(self, member_id, book_id):
        member = self.members[member_id]  # look up member
        book = self.books[book_id]          # look up book
        reason = self.eligibility_strategy.check_eligibility(member, self._active_loan_count(member_id))  # eligibility check
        if reason is not None:  # not eligible
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_loan_rejected(member_id, reason)  # notify
            raise BorrowingNotEligibleException(reason)
        copy = self._find_free_copy(book_id)  # look for a free copy
        if copy is None:  # none free
            self.holds[book_id].append(member_id)  # enqueue FIFO
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_hold_placed(member_id, book_id)  # notify
            return None  # no loan yet, just a hold
        copy.status = CopyStatus.CHECKED_OUT  # claim the copy
        self.loan_counter += 1                  # bump id counter
        loan_id = f"LOAN-{self.loan_counter}"    # build id
        due_day = self.eligibility_strategy.loan_duration_days(book.category)  # duration by category
        loan = Loan(loan_id, member_id, copy.copy_id, book_id, 0, due_day)  # build loan (checkout_day 0 for this demo)
        self.loans[loan_id] = loan  # store it
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_loan_created(loan)  # notify
        return loan  # hand back to caller

    def return_book(self, loan_id, return_day):
        loan = self.loans.get(loan_id)  # look up loan
        if loan is None:
            raise InvalidLoanException(f"Unknown loan: {loan_id}")
        if loan.status != "ACTIVE":
            raise LoanNotActiveException(f"Loan {loan_id} is not active")
        book = self.books[loan.book_id]  # look up book for category
        days_late = max(0, return_day-loan.due_day)  # days beyond due date
        fine = self.eligibility_strategy.fine_for_days_late(book.category, days_late)  # capped fine
        member = self.members[loan.member_id]  # borrower
        member.add_fine(fine)  # accrue the fine
        loan.fine = fine          # record on the loan
        loan.status = "RETURNED"  # mark returned
        copy = self.copies[loan.copy_id]  # the copy this loan held
        copy.status = CopyStatus.AVAILABLE  # free it
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_loan_returned(loan, fine)  # notify
        queue = self.holds[loan.book_id]  # this title's hold queue
        if queue:  # someone is waiting
            promoted_member_id = queue.pop(0)  # longest-waiting member
            copy.status = CopyStatus.CHECKED_OUT  # claim the freed copy
            self.loan_counter += 1                   # bump id counter
            new_loan_id = f"LOAN-{self.loan_counter}"  # build id
            new_due_day = return_day + self.eligibility_strategy.loan_duration_days(book.category)  # fresh due date
            promoted_loan = Loan(new_loan_id, promoted_member_id, copy.copy_id, loan.book_id, return_day, new_due_day)  # build loan
            self.loans[new_loan_id] = promoted_loan  # store it
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_loan_created(promoted_loan)  # notify
        return fine  # hand back to caller

items: Why gate checkout on outstanding fines rather than just loan count? Real libraries use fine balance as a proxy for account standing; a member who never returns anything on time is a collection risk regardless of how many books they currently hold.

Why cap the fine instead of letting it grow indefinitely? An uncapped fine on a lost or forgotten book could grow far past the book's replacement value, which is neither fair to the member nor useful to the library.
How would you support renewing a loan instead of returning it? Add a renew(loanId) method that extends dueDay by the category's loan duration, but only if the book's hold queue is empty.

Fixed loan-limit and fine-limit constants vs per-member-tier configuration: fixed constants are simple to reason about and test, at the cost of not supporting different privileges for staff, students, or premium members; a production system would likely externalize these into per-tier configuration.

Capped linear fine vs no cap: a cap protects members from runaway charges but means the library recovers less on severely overdue or lost books; a real system might combine a capped daily fine with a separate lost-book replacement charge.

Unbounded hold queue vs bounded: unbounded matches how most libraries actually run holds (no limit on how many members can wait for a popular title), unlike Airline Management System's bounded overbooking limit which reflects a physically constrained aircraft.
Persist books, copies, members, and loans in a relational database rather than in-memory maps, using the schema in the Database Design section.
Emit loan/hold/return events to a message queue so downstream systems (email reminders, fine statements) can consume them asynchronously instead of via in-process observers.
Add idempotency keys to checkout so retried network requests cannot create duplicate loans.
Expose metrics on hold-queue length per title to help the library decide which titles need additional copies.
